text:
B: Hiya, love! Oh, I'm ever so glad it's you. I said when I saw your photo, I feel like I know her already.
A: Ha, hiya. Yeah, I thought you looked dead friendly. I'm Kerry, Bridgwater.
B: Joanne, Batley. And I saw your dog lead on the hook. What've you got?
A: Staffie. Roxy. She's an old girl now. Needs her teeth doing at the vet's and it's going to bleed me dry.
B: Oh, don't. We've got Mabel, she's a Border terrier, she's twelve, and I'm not joking, she's started snoring louder than my husband.
A: Ha! That's saying something.
B: It is! So what do you do, love?
A: Painter and decorator. Self-employed, just me.
B: Oh, never! I'm self-employed and all, I'm an upholsterer. I've got a little unit on an industrial estate.
A: Are you? That's proper skilled, that. How long you been doing it?
B: On my own nine years. But I were in a factory from sixteen, so, a long time. You?
A: Eight years on my own. I was in a shoe shop and behind a bar till I was twenty-seven, then I did my NVQs at the college. Best thing I ever did, to be honest. Even if my back don't think so.
B: Oh, I'm the same with my knees. Do you get the customers who want it all for nothing?
A: Oh my God. I've got one now, I've done her front room and her hall, and every time I'm packing up it's, oh, while you're here, could you just do that one wall. Just the one wall. For free, obviously.
B: Just the one wall! I get, oh, can you just re-cover the seat, it'll only take five minutes. And I'm thinking, love, it's got no webbing left in it, it's held together by hope.
A: Ha! Held together by hope. Yeah, and then they say, oh, my mate's fella can do it cheaper.
B: Well, let him, then! I quote honest and if they don't like it, fair enough. But I'm not cutting corners, because it's somebody's nan's chair, do you know what I mean?
A: Yeah. That's it, though. You put your name on it.
B: You do. And then there's waiting for people to pay. That's what keeps me up.
A: Don't. I've got a lettings agent owes me for two jobs. I've got a list in my head of exactly who owes me what. January I'm always panicking.
B: Oh, I put money by every month for the tax, I have to, otherwise I'd never sleep. I nearly lost the business in the pandemic, honestly. I didn't sleep for about a year.
A: God. I bet. I was skint for months.
B: Anyway, I'm rambling. Would you ever take somebody on? An apprentice?
A: Maybe. If I found one who actually turned up. That's the problem, isn't it.
B: That's what I worry about, nobody's learning it. It'll all be flat-pack in twenty years.
A: Yeah. Have you got kids?
B: One, Lewis, he's twenty-three, in Leeds. Comes back for his tea every Sunday.
A: Mine's fourteen. Jayden. I've just been telling the bloke before, I'll be crying in his room when he goes.
B: Oh, you will. I did. I still do sometimes, I'm terrible, I cry at the adverts—
